claims.text: Controlled annealing or thermomechanical heat treatment promotes a more homogeneous distribution of constituent elements in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni high-entropy alloys.
Controlled annealing or thermomechanical heat treatment triggers the formation of finely dispersed ordered nanophases in Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloys.
Homogenization and ordered nanophase formation enhance phase stability.
Improved microstructural uniformity mediates a combination of high-temperature strength, radiation tolerance, environmental resistance, and cryogenic toughness.
The initial as-cast Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni alloy has notable elemental segregation and multiple metastable phases.
An annealing temperature below melting but sufficiently high for diffusion can avoid undesired grain growth while enabling homogenization.
An inert or controlled atmosphere prevents unwanted oxidation during treatment.
Heat treatment enhances elemental diffusion and reduces local chemical inhomogeneity.
Reduced local chemical inhomogeneity lowers the driving force for multiple-phase separation.
Nanoscale precipitates act as pinning centers that hinder grain-boundary motion.
Precipitate-induced inhibition of grain-boundary motion stabilizes phase morphology.
Treated specimens will exhibit either a single more stable phase or a controlled phase mixture containing nanometer-scale dispersions.
Treated specimens will have greater high-temperature strength than untreated as-cast specimens.
Treated specimens will have greater radiation tolerance than untreated as-cast specimens.
Treated specimens will have greater environmental resistance than untreated as-cast specimens.
Treated specimens will have greater cryogenic toughness than untreated as-cast specimens.
Pronounced segregation and multiple metastable phases in the as-cast baseline cause less consistent and inferior performance under varied thermal and mechanical conditions.
The hypothesis is limited to conventional Al–Co–Cr–Fe–Ni composition ranges and treatments that avoid substantial grain coarsening and contamination-derived secondary phases.
The hypothesis may not apply to substantially off-stoichiometric compositions or alloys containing extrinsic alloying elements.
Failure to observe statistically significant homogenization and beneficial nanophase formation together with consistent property improvements would falsify the proposed annealing mechanism.
